title: Quantum codes on a lattice with boundary
authors: Sergey B. Bravyi, Alexei Yu. Kitaev
one_sentence: Extends Kitaev's toric code to lattices with edges and holes, turning a flat 2D chip with boundaries into a topological quantum memory.
contribution: Introduces local-check stabilizer (additive) codes on 2D lattices with two types of boundary conditions: rough and smooth edges. On these lattices, logical operators correspond to relative homology classes instead of non-contractible loops of a closed surface. This is the mathematical origin of the planar surface code and of defect/puncture encodings.
why_it_matters: It is the foundational construction that makes toric-code protection possible on a realistic planar geometry, which every practical surface-code architecture builds on.

title: Topological quantum memory
authors: Eric Dennis, Alexei Kitaev, Andrew Landahl, John Preskill
one_sentence: Shows that, under its local stochastic error models and below a finite threshold, increasing a surface code can make arbitrarily long reliable storage possible with active local syndrome processing.
contribution: Analyzes Kitaev's surface codes as fault-tolerant quantum memories under specified stochastic data and syndrome-error models. It maps decoding to disordered statistical-mechanical models whose ordered phases correspond to correctable regimes, derives model-dependent threshold estimates, and explains how local checks plus global classical decoding can support scalable active error correction.
why_it_matters: It transformed the toric code from a mathematical curiosity into a credible physical memory and introduced the stat-mech mapping that underpins all subsequent surface-code threshold analysis.
verified_note: PDF-verified (plan-v2): under the paper's local stochastic storage model, the accuracy threshold satisfies p_c >= 1.7 x 10^-4 per step. The bound covers reliable storage, not full computation.

title: A fault-tolerant one-way quantum computer
authors: R. Raussendorf, J. Harrington, K. Goyal
one_sentence: Performs fault-tolerant universal quantum computation by single-qubit measurements on a 3D cluster state that behaves like a surface code evolving through time.
contribution: Connects cluster-state (one-way/measurement-based) quantum computation to surface codes. A 3D cluster state with engineered lattice defects provides intrinsic topological error correction. The 'vacuum', 'defect', and 'singular' regions are defined by measurement bases. Estimates thresholds of 1.4% for local depolarizing noise and 0.11% per error source in a full circuit-level model.
why_it_matters: It established a construction-level connection between 3D cluster-state MBQC and histories of topological error correction. It gave an early local topological scheme and laid groundwork for the RHG lattice used in later fault-tolerant architectures.

title: Fault-tolerant quantum computation with high threshold in two dimensions
authors: R. Raussendorf, J. Harrington
one_sentence: Reduces the 3D cluster-state fault-tolerance scheme to a 2D lattice of qubits with only nearest-neighbor Ising interactions, keeping a ~0.75% threshold.
contribution: Converts the one-way quantum computer into a sequential scheme that builds the 3D cluster one slice at a time. This scheme only ever needs a 2D physical lattice with nearest-neighbor interactions, plus single-qubit preparation and measurement. Integrates toric-code topological error correction with magic state distillation, achieving a 0.75% threshold per error source with moderate overhead.
why_it_matters: It made topological fault tolerance compatible with genuinely 2D hardware (optical lattices, ion traps, later superconducting chips), which is the geometry essentially all experimental surface-code efforts use today.

title: Topological fault-tolerance in cluster state quantum computation
authors: R. Raussendorf, J. Harrington, K. Goyal
one_sentence: The long-form version of the RHG scheme: fault-tolerant gates via boundary conditions and defect topology in a 3D cluster state, with tools to simplify circuits topologically.
contribution: Provides the full detailed construction of topologically protected gates in the 3D cluster state. Gates are realized by boundary conditions and defects carved out by Z-measurements. Introduces equivalence transformations for these boundary conditions. These transformations let one simplify fault-tolerant circuits and derive circuit identities in a purely topological manner. Also describes the reduction from 3D to a 2D-plus-time (bi-layer) implementation with a 0.75% threshold and polylogarithmic overhead.
why_it_matters: It is the canonical reference for the defect-based topological cluster-state scheme, and its topological circuit-identities technique is a direct ancestor of modern spacetime/correlation-surface methods for compiling surface-code computations.

title: High threshold universal quantum computation on the surface code
authors: Austin G. Fowler, Ashley M. Stephens, Peter Groszkowski
one_sentence: A self-contained tutorial showing how to run a full universal quantum computer on a single 2D nearest-neighbor lattice by braiding hole defects in the surface code.
contribution: Reframes the Raussendorf-Harrington-Goyal scheme entirely as direct stabilizer manipulation of the 2D surface code. Qubits are encoded in pairs of holes (defects). Logical gates, including long-range CNOTs, are performed by braiding defects via code deformation. Reviews the ~1% threshold, adjustable error-correction strength, and low-overhead long-range logical gates, deliberately avoiding heavy homology language.
why_it_matters: It made the defect-based surface code accessible to the broader quantum community and became the standard entry point for the 'braid holes on a 2D chip' architecture that dominated surface-code thinking for years.

title: Topological cluster state quantum computing
authors: Austin G. Fowler, Kovid Goyal
one_sentence: A simplified re-explanation of the RHG scheme purely as 3D cluster-state stabilizer mechanics, without topology jargon or explicit surface-code language.
contribution: Reviews the Raussendorf-Harrington-Goyal fault-tolerant scheme as a pure cluster-state computation. It describes defect encoding, adjustable-strength error correction (correcting general errors by handling Z errors only), and low-overhead long-range logical gates. It uses only the 3D cluster state and its stabilizers. It assumes no background in cluster states or stabilizers.
why_it_matters: It provides the most pedagogical account of the 3D cluster-state scheme, clarifying the stabilizer-level mechanics of the RHG lattice that later became central to photonic and measurement-based fault-tolerance proposals.

title: Quantum computing with nearest neighbor interactions and error rates over 1%
authors: David S. Wang, Austin G. Fowler, Lloyd C. L. Hollenberg
one_sentence: Pushes the circuit-level surface-code threshold above 1% on a strictly 2D nearest-neighbor lattice by making the decoder aware of detailed error probabilities.
contribution: Performs detailed circuit-level simulations of the surface code with realistic gate, identity, and measurement error models. Feeds approximate error-event probabilities into the minimum-weight matching decoder. Simplifies the syndrome-extraction gate sequence, so qubits no longer need re-initialization. Raises the geometrically constrained threshold to 1.1-1.4%, a 50% improvement over the previous record.
why_it_matters: It demonstrated that thresholds above 1% are achievable under realistic hardware constraints, and pioneered weighted/informed matching decoding, a technique central to all modern surface-code decoders.

title: Towards practical classical processing for the surface code
authors: Austin G. Fowler, Adam C. Whiteside, Lloyd C. L. Hollenberg
one_sentence: Analyzes matching-decoder processing schemes intended to scale with a continuously running surface-code computer; it is an algorithmic architecture result, not a hardware real-time demonstration.
contribution: Studies classical decoding for a fault-tolerant n x n surface-code lattice with imperfect syndrome extraction. It gives serial and locally parallel processing constructions and analyzes average complexity under the paper's stochastic and architectural assumptions, motivating continuous-window and distributed decoding. The asymptotic result does not by itself establish a concrete device's wall-clock throughput or latency.
why_it_matters: It identified classical decoding as a systems problem and showed how local parallel resources could scale with code area in the analyzed model, motivating later real-time implementations and benchmarks.

title: Surface code quantum computing by lattice surgery
authors: Dominic Horsman, Austin G. Fowler, Simon Devitt, Rodney Van Meter
one_sentence: Introduces lattice surgery - merging and splitting planar surface-code patches - to do logical gates without braiding defects or long-range transversal gates.
contribution: Introduces the lattice surgery technique for coupling planar (single-logical-qubit) surface codes. Merging and splitting surfaces along boundaries implements logical measurements and a CNOT. This preserves the strictly 2D nearest-neighbor structure and removes the need for braided defect logic and transversal operations. Uses rotated planar encodings to cut qubit overhead. Shows efficient distribution of encoded GHZ states. Demonstrates an encoded distance-3 CNOT with just 53 physical qubits - half of any previous 2D construction.
why_it_matters: Lattice surgery became an influential basis for many surface-code resource estimates, compiler designs, and experimental roadmaps, while defect, twist, transversal, and other architectures remain active alternatives.
verified_note: PDF-verified (plan-v2) merge convention: a rough merge measures X_L X_L, and a smooth merge measures Z_L Z_L.

title: Proof of finite surface code threshold for matching
authors: Austin G. Fowler
one_sentence: Rigorously proves that a 2D nearest-neighbor surface code with minimum-weight matching decoding has a finite fault-tolerance threshold of at least 7.4 x 10^-4 per operation.
contribution: Provides a formal finite-threshold proof for a specified local two-dimensional surface-code circuit and stochastic fault model with noisy gates, preparation, and measurement. Decoding uses minimum-weight matching. The conservative proved bound p < 7.4 x 10^-4 gives asymptotic suppression within those assumptions; it is not a universal threshold for arbitrary realistic hardware noise.
why_it_matters: It put the surface code's fault tolerance on rigorous mathematical footing, giving the field a proven (not just simulated) guarantee that local 2D hardware suffices for scalable quantum computing.

title: Surface codes: Towards practical large-scale quantum computation
authors: Austin G. Fowler, Matteo Mariantoni, John M. Martinis, Andrew N. Cleland
one_sentence: The comprehensive, pedagogical review of defect-based surface-code quantum computing, co-written with the superconducting-qubit experimentalists who would go on to build it.
contribution: A start-to-finish tutorial on surface-code quantum computing. It estimates the size and speed of a surface-code machine. It builds up stabilizers and the surface code from scratch. It explains logical qubits via defects, fault-tolerance numerics, logical qubit movement, braiding-based CNOTs, and the full universal gate set including state distillation. Appendices cover implementation details. Written assuming only basic quantum mechanics and circuits background, with an eye toward superconducting-qubit realizations.
why_it_matters: It is the canonical 'textbook chapter' of the defect-based surface-code era and a key theory-experiment bridge - the Martinis/Cleland collaboration directly foreshadowed the Google/UCSB superconducting surface-code experiments.
verified_note: PDF-verified (plan-v2): the worked example factors an N = 2000-bit number with about a billion physical qubits running for about one day; state distillation dominates the footprint.

title: A bridge to lower overhead quantum computation
authors: Austin G. Fowler, Simon J. Devitt
one_sentence: A technique called bridge compression that shrinks the 3-D spacetime 'plumbing' of defect-based surface-code computations, drastically cutting the number of physical qubits needed.
contribution: Introduces bridge compression, a method for deforming the spacetime defect structures of surface-code computations into far more compact equivalent forms. Applied to state distillation circuits (e.g. the 7-to-1 |Y> and 15-to-1 |A> distillation), it reduces the qubit-time volume by large factors. This shows that defect-based surface-code computation can have reasonable overhead. The paper also gives a clear argument for why topological schemes (volume scaling as n_f^3) beat concatenated codes (n_f^10) at scale.
why_it_matters: It made defect-based surface-code computation look practically affordable for the first time, turning scary overhead estimates into plausible engineering numbers. It is the canonical reference for thinking of a surface-code computation as a 3-D topological structure that can be reshaped without changing what it computes.

title: Time-optimal quantum computation
authors: Austin G. Fowler
one_sentence: Shows that, with abundant space plus sufficiently fast classical processing and communication, a fault-tolerant Clifford+T layer can be organized around one physical-measurement reaction step.
contribution: Introduces selective-destination and selective-source teleportation gadgets. These gadgets execute an arbitrary Clifford circuit, a layer of independent T gates, and feed-forward corrective S gates in the time of one physical measurement. The runtime becomes independent of the error-correction strength (code distance), assuming fast classical processing and communication. Applied to the surface code, it removes the large serial time overhead previously associated with defect-based T gates and their measurement-dependent corrections.
why_it_matters: It exposed a space-for-time tradeoff and helped motivate reaction-limited computation. Its time-optimal claim depends on abundant ancillas, routing, and sufficiently fast classical processing and communication rather than applying to every architecture.

title: Minimum weight perfect matching of fault-tolerant topological quantum error correction in average O(1) parallel time
authors: Austin G. Fowler
one_sentence: Gives an average-O(1)-per-round parallel matching construction under a specified local processor array and stochastic operating model.
contribution: Gives a rigorous proof for minimum weight perfect matching (MWPM) decoding of topological codes with local stabilizers. The proof includes the fully fault-tolerant case with imperfect stabilizer measurements. A 2-D array of classical computing devices can perform this decoding in average O(1) time per round of error detection, independent of lattice size L. The serial version of the algorithm runs in average O(n) and worst-case O(n^2) time in the number of detection events. This is the optimal possible scaling for a continuously running quantum computer.
why_it_matters: It showed that matching admits favorable parallel scaling under the paper's architecture and average-case assumptions. Concrete real-time feasibility still depends on graph construction, constants, communication, hardware, latency, and the actual noise stream.

title: Optimal complexity correction of correlated errors in the surface code
authors: Austin G. Fowler
one_sentence: Shows how to decode the surface code better by exploiting the fact that X and Z errors are correlated (e.g. depolarizing noise), using a reweighting trick on top of minimum weight perfect matching.
contribution: Introduces a correlated decoding strategy. After an initial MWPM pass, the decoder uses high-confidence matched edges to infer likely errors of the other Pauli type. This works because depolarizing noise produces Y errors. It then reweights the matching graph and matches it again. This is the first treatment of error-correlation exploitation in the realistic setting of a 2-D lattice with nearest-neighbor gates and no perfect operations. The algorithm retains optimal complexity (linear, parallelizable to O(1)). For depolarizing error rates below ~2 x 10^-4, it performs almost as well as the asymptotically optimal decoder.
why_it_matters: Correlated decoding meaningfully improves logical error rates and effective thresholds for free, and the reweighting idea is the ancestor of modern correlated and ensemble decoders used in today's surface-code experiments. It demonstrates that decoding is not a solved, fixed subroutine but a place to win real performance.

title: Logic gates at the surface code threshold: Superconducting qubits poised for fault-tolerant quantum computing
authors: R. Barends, J. Kelly, et al. (UCSB / Google, John M. Martinis group)
one_sentence: The Martinis group's five-qubit superconducting device demonstrated a universal physical gate set with fidelities comparable to surface-code threshold estimates from specified models.
contribution: Demonstrates a universal set of logic gates on a linear array of five Xmon transmon qubits with nearest-neighbor coupling. Clifford-based randomized benchmarking verifies an average single-qubit gate fidelity of 99.92% and two-qubit controlled-Z gate fidelity up to 99.4%. The fast-adiabatic CZ gate suppresses leakage while remaining quick, and simultaneous operation on nearest/next-nearest qubits adds errors below 2 x 10^-4. A five-qubit GHZ state is constructed as a full-circuit demonstration.
why_it_matters: It showed strong physical gate performance and an architecture suitable for scaling experiments. It did not run an encoded surface code or demonstrate below-threshold logical error correction: randomized-benchmarking fidelities cannot be compared to one universal threshold without a circuit and noise model.

title: Low overhead quantum computation using lattice surgery
authors: Austin G. Fowler, Craig Gidney
one_sentence: Replaces defect braiding with lattice surgery on rotated surface-code patches and shows this cuts the qubit overhead of large fault-tolerant computations by roughly a factor of 4-5.
contribution: Systematically develops the lattice-surgery toolkit: rotated logical qubit storage, logical initialization and measurement, and multi-qubit logical XX and ZZ parity measurements via merge/split. Uses this toolkit to re-cost full algorithms including magic-state distillation. Storage drops from ~12.5d^2 to ~3d^2 physical qubits per logical qubit. Distillation overhead falls by nearly a factor of 5. This enables algorithms with 10^8 T gates on ~3.7 x 10^5 physical qubits at p ~ 10^-3. The authors explicitly argue defects and braids should be deprecated in favor of lattice surgery.
why_it_matters: This paper helped shift many surface-code architecture studies from defect braiding toward lattice surgery. Its concrete estimates set an influential template, while their numerical advantages remain tied to the paper's layouts, workloads, and physical-error assumptions.

title: Efficient magic state factories with a catalyzed |CCZ> to 2|T> transformation
authors: Craig Gidney, Austin G. Fowler
one_sentence: Builds smaller, faster magic-state factories by distilling CCZ states directly and then converting each CCZ into two T states using a catalyst T state that is returned at the end.
contribution: Applies surface-code lattice-surgery techniques to construct a |CCZ> factory with the paper's stated footprint and cadence. Its ideal catalyzed phasing circuit converts one |CCZ> resource into two T-type outputs while returning a T-type catalyst. At the noisy-factory level, catalyst errors can persist or correlate later outputs, so throughput and marginal-error headlines do not by themselves model catalyst history, acceptance, or logical circuit faults. The reported footprint and speed comparisons are scoped to the analyzed layouts.
why_it_matters: Magic-resource production dominates some surface-code workloads and resource estimates. The paper showed that CCZ-focused factories and catalytic conversion can lower cost in analyzed Toffoli-heavy layouts, while the advantage remains architecture-, workload-, and error-budget-dependent.

title: Flexible layout of surface code computations using AutoCCZ states
authors: Craig Gidney, Austin G. Fowler
one_sentence: Introduces an augmented AutoCCZ resource state whose ancillas support delayed-choice fixups, then uses it in compact reaction-limited surface-code layouts.
contribution: Constructs the AutoCCZ state with embedded delayed-choice CZs for completing gate teleportations. This reduces the spacetime volume of delayed-choice CZs by a factor of 4 relative to Fowler's 2012 selective-routing technique. Using it, the authors lay out complete computations (a ripple-carry adder and a QROM read) including distillation and routing under plausible superconducting-qubit assumptions. They show that circuit-level Toffoli parallelism gives no speedup below ~5 million physical qubits. The paper unifies circuit diagrams, ZX calculus, and 3-D topological diagrams as equivalent views of lattice-surgery computations.
why_it_matters: It matured the 'reaction-limited computation' paradigm for lattice-surgery machines, showing how entire algorithms (not just gates) are arranged as spacetime structures and what actually limits their speed. These layout and AutoCCZ techniques feed directly into modern end-to-end resource estimates for fault-tolerant algorithms.

title: Suppressing quantum errors by scaling a surface code logical qubit
authors: Google Quantum AI
one_sentence: Google reported the first larger-code surface-memory comparison, with a modest average distance-5 improvement over distance 3 on its 2022 hardware.
contribution: Implements distance-3 and distance-5 surface-code memories on a 72-qubit superconducting Sycamore device. Measures logical performance across 25 error-correction cycles. The distance-5 code modestly outperforms the average of distance-3 codes (2.914% vs 3.028% logical error per cycle). A distance-25 repetition code probes rare damaging events, revealing a 1.7 x 10^-6 logical error floor set by a single high-energy event. Accurate device modeling enables error budgets that identify the dominant challenges for future systems.
why_it_matters: It was an important first larger-code comparison and exposed rare correlated events as a key obstacle. Two tested distances with a modest average improvement did not by themselves establish exponential suppression; the later d=3,5,7 Willow study supplied the clearer scaling evidence.

title: Quantum error correction below the surface code threshold
authors: Google Quantum AI and Collaborators
one_sentence: Google demonstrated clear below-threshold scaling across distance-3, 5, and 7 surface-code memories, plus a distance-5 real-time decoding experiment and a separate beyond-break-even lifetime comparison.
contribution: Realizes a 101-qubit distance-7 surface-code memory and a distance-5 memory with integrated real-time decoding. With Lambda defined as epsilon(d)/epsilon(d+2), it reports Lambda = 2.14 +/- 0.02 per +2 increase in distance and 0.143 +/- 0.003% logical error per cycle at distance 7. Separately, the distance-7 encoded lifetime exceeds that of its best constituent physical qubit by 2.4 +/- 0.3; this lifetime ratio is not Lambda. Real-time decoding reports 63 microsecond average latency while sustaining a pipelined 1.1 microsecond cycle stream. Repetition-code experiments probe rare correlated events and an observed low-error floor in that setup.
why_it_matters: It supplied clear memory-scaling evidence across three distances and an important real-time decoding benchmark under a declared circuit and decoder. It does not by itself demonstrate a universal fault-tolerant gate set or an end-to-end algorithm, and its fitted scaling should not be generalized to arbitrary hardware or workloads.

title: Surface code off-the-hook: diagonal syndrome-extraction scheduling
authors: Gilad Kishony, Austin Fowler
one_sentence: A new 'diagonal' ordering of the gates in surface-code syndrome extraction that tames hook errors uniformly everywhere, simplifying circuits and shortening each error-correction cycle from 7 steps to 6.
contribution: Proposes a diagonal syndrome-extraction schedule for analyzed rotated-surface-code memories and deformation primitives. The four two-qubit-gate layers orient propagated hook errors along plaquette diagonals; the paper verifies distance preservation for its stated boundary geometries and circuits rather than establishing a geometry-independent rule for every code. Under its parallel measurement/reset timing model it gives a six-step period, and simulations compare logical performance for the studied memory and lattice-surgery primitives.
why_it_matters: It represents the state of the art in surface-code circuit engineering: squeezing depth and complexity out of the fundamental error-correction cycle while provably maintaining fault-tolerance distance. Such circuit-level simplifications directly translate into faster cycles and easier compilation of large lattice-surgery computations.

title: The ZX calculus is a language for surface code lattice surgery
authors: Niel de Beaudrap and Dominic Horsman
one_sentence: It shows that the merge-and-split operations of surface-code lattice surgery are exactly the 'spiders' of the ZX calculus, so whole fault-tolerant computations can be drawn and reasoned about as topological ZX diagrams.
contribution: The paper gives a precise dictionary between lattice surgery operations (merges, splits, CNOTs, Hadamards, phase gates, state injection) and ZX-calculus generators, proving that every ZX diagram built from these operations has an operational reading as a lattice surgery procedure. It also shows how ZX rewrite rules such as spider fusion correspond to valid manipulations of surface-code computations, including the cancellation of a merge followed by a split.
why_it_matters: This is the conceptual foundation of TQEC design automation: it turns fault-tolerant circuit compilation into diagrammatic rewriting on ZX graphs, the representation later used by compilers such as tqec and TopoLS.

title: PyZX: Large Scale Automated Diagrammatic Reasoning
authors: Aleks Kissinger and John van de Wetering
one_sentence: PyZX is a Python library that automatically simplifies, optimizes, and verifies quantum circuits by rewriting them as large ZX diagrams.
contribution: The paper introduces PyZX, an open-source tool that converts quantum circuits to ZX diagrams, applies scalable rewrite strategies (spider fusion, local complementation and pivoting for Clifford simplification, phase gadget elimination for T-count reduction), and extracts optimized circuits back. It demonstrates circuit optimization and efficient equivalence validation on benchmark suites of tens of thousands of gates.
why_it_matters: PyZX is the workhorse ZX-calculus engine that later TQEC compilers rely on for circuit-level optimization and for manipulating the diagrammatic intermediate representation of lattice surgery programs.

title: Stim: a fast stabilizer circuit simulator
authors: Craig Gidney
one_sentence: Stim is a very fast open-source simulator for noisy stabilizer circuits, able to analyze a distance-100 surface code circuit in seconds and then sample millions of shots.
contribution: Stim improves the Aaronson-Gottesman stabilizer tableau simulation by separating the circuit into a bulk stabilizer part (applied via fast bit-packed operations with greatly improved asymptotic cost) and a non-stabilizer part (measurements), and by analyzing a circuit's error channels once to compute a detector/observable reference sample for frame-based sampling. It supports detector and logical observable annotations, making it a natural fit for QEC circuit experiments.
why_it_matters: Stim became the de facto file format and simulation backend for the whole TQEC toolchain: compilers like tqec emit Stim circuits, and decoders and resource estimators consume them.

title: Parallel window decoding enables scalable fault tolerant quantum computation
authors: Luka Skoric et al.
one_sentence: It shows that decoding can be split into overlapping spacetime 'windows' that are decoded in parallel and merged at the end, so a single logical qubit can be decoded in real time at any code distance.
contribution: The authors prove that the decoding graph of a surface code memory experiment can be partitioned into overlapping windows processed independently, with only a small buffer region around each window, without loss of logical fidelity. They show this removes the backlog problem of streaming decoders, and extend the scheme to logical measurements and lattice surgery operations.
why_it_matters: Parallel window decoding is the key algorithmic idea that makes real-time decoding scale with code distance and with the number of logical qubits; later real-time decoder architectures, including Google's, build on it.

title: A High Performance Compiler for Very Large Scale Surface Code Computations
authors: George Watkins et al.
one_sentence: liblsqecc is an open-source compiler that turns arbitrary logical quantum circuits into lattice surgery instructions on a surface-code architecture, handling layout, routing, and magic state distillation automatically.
contribution: The paper presents a complete compilation pipeline: scheduling of lattice surgery operations, qubit layout synthesis with routing-aware heuristics, integration of Litinski-style multi-body measurement decomposition, and automatic inclusion of magic state factories. It compiles large benchmark algorithms in minutes to hours and reports space-time volumes, enabling quantitative architecture studies.
why_it_matters: It was the first practical open-source end-to-end compiler for large-scale lattice surgery, setting the baseline against which later compilers (DASCOT, TopoLS) measure space-time volume improvements.

title: Sparse Blossom: correcting a million errors per core second with minimum-weight matching
authors: Oscar Higgott and Craig Gidney
one_sentence: Sparse Blossom is a dramatically faster implementation of the minimum-weight perfect matching decoder, correcting over a million surface-code errors per second on one CPU core.
contribution: The authors reformulate the blossom algorithm to operate directly on the sparse syndrome graph rather than a dense graph of detection events, using an adaptive Dijkstra-style search and local data structures so the cost scales with the number of detection events, not the code size. The implementation (PyMatching 2) achieves orders-of-magnitude speedups over previous MWPM decoders and approaches linear average-case runtime.
why_it_matters: Sparse Blossom made accurate MWPM decoding fast enough for the large-scale simulations that drive TQEC design-space exploration, and is the accuracy baseline for nearly every decoder and compiler study since.

title: Fusion Blossom: Fast MWPM Decoders for QEC
authors: Yue Wu and Lin Zhong
one_sentence: Fusion Blossom parallelizes minimum-weight perfect matching decoding by recursively splitting the decoding problem, solving the parts independently, and fusing their solutions along a precomputed tree.
contribution: The paper introduces two ideas: Parity Blossom, a fast sequential MWPM variant that exploits the sparse syndrome-graph construction, and a divide-and-fuse scheme that partitions the decoding graph using an offline-computed tree structure so sub-problems can be solved in parallel and their boundary solutions merged. It reports near-linear scaling of throughput with the number of parallel units and decoding of a distance-33 surface code in under a microsecond per round in parallel configurations.
why_it_matters: Fusion Blossom demonstrates that high-accuracy matching decoders can be parallelized across hardware, a blueprint followed by FPGA and networked real-time decoding systems such as Helios and DECONET.

title: Dependency-Aware Compilation for Surface Code Quantum Architectures
authors: Abtin Molavi et al.
one_sentence: DASCOT compiles circuits to lattice surgery by extracting the dependency graph of multi-qubit measurements and searching over layouts and schedules, rather than compiling gate-by-gate.
contribution: The authors formulate lattice surgery compilation around the dependency structure of Pauli product measurements, enabling reordering and parallelization that gate-centric compilers miss, and combine this with search-based techniques for qubit placement and routing on a 2D grid. They show significant reductions in space-time volume and compilation improvements over liblsqecc-style pipelines.
why_it_matters: It shifts TQEC compilation from circuit transcription to optimization over the program's intrinsic dependency structure, an intermediate step toward fully topology-centric compilers like TopoLS.

title: Spatially parallel decoding for multi-qubit lattice surgery
authors: Sophia Fuhui Lin et al.
one_sentence: It extends parallel window decoding into space, so that the decoding graph of many logical qubits undergoing lattice surgery can be split into spatial regions decoded in parallel with bounded inter-region communication.
contribution: The paper generalizes time-wise parallel windows to spatial windows that partition a multi-logical-qubit decoding problem, analyzing how windows overlap and how intermediate solutions are passed between adjacent windows. It shows analytically that inter-window communication latency does not create a scalability bottleneck and evaluates accuracy-latency tradeoffs for lattice surgery decoding workloads.
why_it_matters: Spatial parallelization is what lets real-time decoding follow an actual computation rather than a single memory experiment, and it underpins distributed decoder systems such as DECONET.

title: A SAT Scalpel for Lattice Surgery: Representation and Synthesis of Subroutines for Surface-Code Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing
authors: Daniel Bochen Tan, Murphy Yuezhen Niu, and Craig Gidney
one_sentence: LaSsynth encodes the design of lattice surgery subroutines as SAT problems and solves for space-time-optimal, provably fault-tolerant constructions that humans had not found.
contribution: The authors develop a compact SAT encoding of lattice surgery operations as 3D space-time volumes subject to topological and fault-tolerance constraints, and use a SAT solver to synthesize optimal subroutine layouts such as multi-qubit measurements and state initialization. They verify fault tolerance of the synthesized constructions and report designs that are smaller in space-time volume than previously known hand-designed ones.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates that core TQEC building blocks can be discovered and proven correct by automated formal synthesis, replacing manual engineering of lattice surgery subroutines.

title: FPGA-based Distributed Union-Find Decoder for Surface Codes
authors: Namitha Liyanage et al.
one_sentence: Helios distributes the Union-Find decoder across a graph of processing elements on an FPGA, achieving decoding times that actually get faster per round as the surface code distance grows.
contribution: The paper presents a distributed implementation of the Union-Find decoder in which the decoding graph is mapped onto a grid of simple processing units that grow and merge clusters locally, achieving sublinear average decoding latency per measurement round in the code distance. On a Xilinx FPGA it decodes a distance-21 surface code in about 11.5 ns per round on average, far below the ~1 microsecond syndrome cycle time of superconducting hardware.
why_it_matters: Helios shows real-time decoding can be both fast and hardware-scalable with lightweight algorithm-hardware co-design, and it serves as the per-qubit decoder engine inside the networked DECONET system.

title: Magic state cultivation: growing T states as cheap as CNOT gates
authors: Craig Gidney, Noah Shutty, and Cody Jones
one_sentence: Magic state cultivation prepares high-fidelity T states by injecting a noisy state into a small color code and gradually growing and postselecting it, at a cost comparable to a single lattice surgery CNOT.
contribution: The paper introduces a complete cultivation protocol: unitary injection into a distance-3 color code, fault-tolerant measurement of the logical Hadamard-basis observable to postselect on state quality, staged code growth with escape to the surface code, and careful error accounting via a mix of state-vector, stabilizer, and enumerative simulation. It estimates T-state infidelities around 1e-9 with spacetime cost similar to a same-distance lattice surgery CNOT, orders of magnitude cheaper than traditional distillation factories.
why_it_matters: Cultivation collapses the cost of magic states, historically the dominant resource in surface-code architectures, and has become a central benchmark and design target for TQEC simulators and compilers.

title: High Rate Magic State Cultivation on the Surface Code
authors: Yotam Vaknin et al.
one_sentence: It adapts magic state cultivation to run directly on the surface code, using non-local connectivity to boost the success probability of growing high-fidelity T states.
contribution: The authors present a cultivation protocol that avoids the detour through the color code, performing injection, verification, and growth natively on surface code patches and exploiting flexible, non-local connectivity (as available in neutral atoms or shuttling architectures) to increase postselection acceptance rates. They analyze the fidelity-rate tradeoff and show higher effective magic state production rates than color-code cultivation at comparable fidelity.
why_it_matters: By cultivating directly in the surface code, it simplifies integration of cheap magic states into mainstream surface-code architectures, tightening the link between magic state factories and lattice surgery compilation.

title: Network-Integrated Decoding System for Real-Time Quantum Error Correction with Lattice Surgery
authors: Namitha Liyanage et al.
one_sentence: DECONET networks multiple FPGAs into a hybrid tree-grid system that decodes hundreds of interacting logical qubits, including lattice surgery operations, in real time.
contribution: DECONET partitions the global decoding graph into per-logical-qubit blocks decoded by separate instances (e.g., Helios), then combines them using fusion within a node and window-based methods across a network-integrated hybrid tree-grid topology, scaling to l logical qubits with O(l log l) compute and only O(log l) latency growth. A five-FPGA prototype decodes 100 distance-5 logical qubits with lattice surgery at 2.4 microseconds average latency and 0.84 microseconds inverse throughput per round.
why_it_matters: It is the first real-time decoding system demonstrated for full multi-logical-qubit computations rather than isolated memories, closing the loop between lattice surgery compilation and decoding hardware.

title: Cultivating T states on the surface code with only two-qubit gates
authors: Jahan Claes
one_sentence: It shows how to cultivate high-fidelity T states directly on the ordinary planar surface code using only two-qubit gates and rigid qubit-array translations, with no mid-circuit measurement, suiting neutral-atom hardware.
contribution: The protocol combines RP2-cultivation ideas with a mid-cycle trick that deforms the surface code mid-syndrome-round into a self-dual code, enabling fault-tolerant measurement of the Hadamard-basis logical operator for postselection, then escapes to larger distances. Under depolarizing noise, d=3/4/5 cultivation reaches error rates of 1e-6/1e-8/2e-9 with acceptance rates of 34%/6%/1%, competitive with or better than color and RP2 cultivation, and works at any distance parity.
why_it_matters: It brings cultivation's magic-state cost savings to the plain surface code under restrictive hardware primitives, widening the architectural design space that TQEC compilers must target.

title: Simulating magic state cultivation with few Clifford terms
authors: Kwok Ho Wan, Zhenghao Zhong, and Ainhoa Zapirain
one_sentence: It shows that the non-Clifford d=5 cultivation circuit can be simulated exactly with only about 8 Clifford ZX-diagram terms on average, instead of millions of stabilizer terms.
contribution: Building on ZX-calculus cutting techniques, the authors construct compact stabilizer-rank decompositions of the 53 non-Clifford spiders in the d=5 magic state cultivation circuit, reducing a naive 6.4-million-term decomposition to about 8 Clifford terms on average at 0.1% noise. Combined with the tsim simulator, they achieve near-Stim sampling speeds for the true non-Clifford circuits, enabling exact simulation of the cultivation circuit itself, with the decomposition designed to remain tractable when the state is ported into the escape stage.
why_it_matters: It demonstrates that ZX-based decomposition can make exact classical verification of operationally important non-Clifford QEC circuits tractable, a key validation tool for automated fault-tolerant design.

title: A scalable and real-time neural decoder for topological quantum codes
authors: Andrew W. Senior et al. (Google DeepMind and Google Quantum AI)
one_sentence: AlphaQubit 2 is a recurrent-transformer neural decoder that achieves near-optimal accuracy on surface and colour codes up to distance 23 while a compact variant decodes in under 1 microsecond per cycle on commercial TPUs.
contribution: AQ2 uses a streaming architecture of interleaved per-stabilizer recurrent layers and attention-based spatial mixing layers with temporal compression, giving constant cost per cycle and stable performance on million-cycle experiments. It reaches logical error rates near 1e-10 per cycle at large distance, orders of magnitude faster than other high-accuracy decoders for the colour code, and its real-time variant AQ2-RT beats leading real-time decoders on accuracy while meeting the 1 microsecond superconducting cycle budget up to distance 11.
why_it_matters: It establishes machine-learned decoding as a credible component of the real-time TQEC stack, simultaneously satisfying the accuracy, speed, and scalability requirements that had previously been met only separately.

title: SOFT: a high-performance simulator for universal fault-tolerant quantum circuits
authors: Riling Li et al.
one_sentence: SOFT is a GPU simulator that runs noisy Clifford+T fault-tolerant circuits with mid-circuit measurements billions of shots at a time, delivering the first ground-truth simulation of d=5 magic state cultivation.
contribution: SOFT integrates the generalized stabilizer formalism with a fully device-resident, shot-parallel GPU design that updates generalized stabilizer tableaux via lightweight staged kernels, achieving orders-of-magnitude speedups over existing simulators for noisy non-Clifford circuits. Simulating the d=5 cultivation circuit (42 qubits, 72 T gates) over 200+ billion shots, it confirmed cultivation's effectiveness while revealing discrepancies of up to ~8x between the true logical error rate and earlier Clifford-proxy estimates.
why_it_matters: It moves TQEC verification from simulating quantum memory to simulating full non-Clifford logical protocols, and its cultivation results shows that proxy-based estimates can misestimate logical error rates by up to ~8x, making the case that resource estimates need ground-truth simulation checks proxy-based resource estimates.

title: TopoLS: Lattice Surgery Compilation via Topological Program Transformations
authors: Junyu Zhou et al.
one_sentence: TopoLS compiles lattice surgery programs topology-first: it rewrites the circuit as a ZX diagram and uses Monte Carlo tree search to embed it into 3D space-time, cutting space-time volume by 46% on average over prior compilers.
contribution: TopoLS uses ZX diagrams as the compilation IR, applying semantics-preserving transformations (spider fusion, topology-aware slicing) to expose merge-split parallelism invisible to gate-centric compilers, then synthesizes pipe-diagram layouts with MCTS that jointly optimizes placement and routing in 3D space-time, with topology-aware partitioning for scalability. Across benchmarks it reduces space-time volume by 25-90% over liblsqecc and DASCOT with near-linear compilation-time scaling, and it is integrated into the tqec ecosystem.
why_it_matters: It realizes the ZX-calculus vision of lattice surgery as a topology-centric compilation target and connects search-based synthesis directly into the tqec design-automation pipeline.

title: Tsim: Fast Universal Simulator for Quantum Error Correction
authors: Rafael Haenel, Xiuzhe Luo, and Chen Zhao
one_sentence: Tsim is QuEra's open-source simulator that compiles noisy universal circuits, written as ZX diagrams with parameterized Pauli-noise vertices, into a vectorized GPU sampler that extends the Stim format with T gates and rotations.
contribution: Tsim represents circuits as ZX diagrams, simplifies them with parameterized ZX rewrite rules, and compiles once for vectorized sampling whose cost is linear in Clifford gates and exponential only in non-Clifford gates. It implements the Stim API and circuit format with non-Clifford extensions, enabling high-throughput exact simulation of low-magic QEC workloads such as magic state cultivation.
why_it_matters: It is a key member of the post-cultivation generation of simulators that let designers verify true non-Clifford fault-tolerant circuits at scale inside a Stim-compatible toolchain.

title: Clifft: Fast Exact Simulation of Near-Clifford Quantum Circuits
authors: Bradley Chase and Farrokh Labib (Unitary Foundation)
one_sentence: Clifft exactly simulates near-Clifford fault-tolerant circuits on ordinary CPUs by tracking the Clifford structure symbolically and keeping a dense state vector only for the dynamically active non-Clifford degrees of freedom.
contribution: Clifft factors the quantum state into an offline Clifford frame, an online Pauli frame, and a dynamically sized active state vector, generalizing Stim's compile-once-sample-many model to circuits with non-Clifford operations; the dominant exponential cost scales with the peak active dimension rather than the qubit count. It achieves up to orders-of-magnitude throughput gains over GPU near-Clifford simulators and performed, to the authors' knowledge, the first exact end-to-end simulation of magic state cultivation including the escape stage, over hundreds of billions of shots.
why_it_matters: It makes exact verification of low-magic fault-tolerant protocols practical on commodity hardware, turning ground-truth checking of compiler outputs into a routine design-automation step.

title: SymFT: Universal Fault-Tolerant Quantum Circuit Simulation via Symbolic Clifford-Pauli Frames and Stabilizer Coordinates
authors: Wang Fang, Huazhe Lou, and Riling Li
one_sentence: SymFT combines symbolic Clifford-Pauli frame factorization with adaptive stabilizer-coordinate planning to sample Clifford-dominated fault-tolerant circuits faster than Stim and Clifft on a single CPU core.
contribution: SymFT reduces branch-probability sampling to Pauli rotations and measurement projectors by pushing residual Clifford and Pauli frames into symbolic signs that need not be applied per shot, and plans a shared stabilizer-destabilizer coordinate basis once, emitting direct multi-coordinate sampling instructions that avoid per-shot tableau updates. It reports 2.5x speedups over Stim on surface-code circuits and 1.9-3.5x over Clifft on cultivation and distillation circuits, and over 100x over its predecessor SOFT.
why_it_matters: It represents the leading edge of simulator co-design, where frame-based symbolic techniques collapse the per-shot cost of verifying universal fault-tolerant circuits for TQEC design iteration.

title: tqec: A Python package for topological quantum error correction
authors: Adrien Suau et al. (15 authors, incl. Austin Fowler)
one_sentence: tqec (DOI: 10.21105/joss.09142, JOSS 11(120), 9142) is an open-source Python compiler that translates a logical computation drawn as connected 3D primitive blocks into a detailed fault-tolerant Stim circuit ready for simulation and decoding.
contribution: The tqec package automates compilation of surface-code and lattice-surgery computations: users specify them as block graphs of 3D topological primitives (its native BlockGraph structure), and the tool instantiates each block with syndrome-extraction circuits using multiple spatial junction types and stretched stabilizers for hook-error handling, emitting Stim circuits with the detector and observable information needed for simulation and decoding, including automated correlation-surface finding.
why_it_matters: It is the reference open-source toolchain of TQEC design automation, with a growing ecosystem around it — including the PyZX interface Topologiq — and it defines the block-graph representation that newer compilers build on.

title: Efficient Magic State Cultivation on RP^2
authors: Zi-Han Chen, Ming-Cheng Chen, Chao-Yang Lu, Jian-Wei Pan
one_sentence: Grows high-fidelity logical T states on a surface code wrapped around the real projective plane (RP^2), cutting the space-time cost of magic state cultivation by about an order of magnitude.
contribution: Introduces the RP^2 code family (rotated surface codes placed on the real projective plane) together with two self-dual CSS codes, SRP-3 and SRP-5, plus fast 'morphing' circuits that switch between them so the logical T state can be double-checked efficiently. A one-round, easy-to-decode expansion stage grows the small RP^2 code directly into a large rotated surface code, avoiding the costly grafting step of the original cultivation protocol. Monte Carlo sampling shows roughly 10x lower space-time volume than the original magic state cultivation protocol at target logical error rates of ~1e-6 to 1e-9, using non-local connectivity available on neutral-atom and ion-trap platforms.
why_it_matters: It is the first cultivation variant shown to beat the original protocol's space-time cost, showing that clever code geometry (RP2 plus non-local connectivity) can remove the grafting bottleneck and that clever code geometry can remove the grafting bottleneck. Published as PRX Quantum 7, 010315 (2026), it anchors the cultivation-variant literature.

title: Magic State Injection with Erasure Qubits
authors: Shoham Jacoby, Yotam Vaknin, Alex Retzker, Arne L. Grimsmo
one_sentence: Shows that qubits whose errors are heralded as erasures make magic state injection and cultivation dramatically cleaner at almost no extra cost.
contribution: Extends magic state injection protocols on the surface code, and injection-plus-cultivation on the color code, to erasure qubits, proving that after postselecting on erasures the logical error rate is set only by the much smaller residual Pauli error while the acceptance rate barely drops. For surface-code injection, just three strategically placed erasure qubits capture almost all of the benefit, independent of patch size; for color-code cultivation, making the whole patch erasure qubits yields about a thousandfold logical-error-rate improvement in simulated regimes. The analysis suggests algorithmically relevant logical error rates without distillation for erasure rates below ~4e-3 and residual Pauli errors ~1e-4.
why_it_matters: It ties the cultivation pipeline to erasure-qubit hardware (e.g., neutral atoms with erasure conversion), showing cultivation can reach distillation-grade fidelities on near-term platforms. It reframes injection—the first stage of every cultivation protocol—as the highest-leverage place to spend heralded-erasure resources.

title: Efficient magic state cultivation with lattice surgery
authors: Yutaka Hirano, Riki Toshio, Tomohiro Itogawa, Keisuke Fujii
one_sentence: Replaces the awkward grafting step of magic state cultivation with ordinary lattice surgery, halving the space-time overhead while staying on a square grid.
contribution: Proposes MSC-LS, a cultivation protocol that keeps the injection and cultivation stages of the original color-code scheme but teleports the cultivated magic state onto a rotated surface code via a zero-level-distillation-style lattice-surgery merge, avoiding the grafted code entirely. Three ideas drive the efficiency: using the space-efficient rotated surface code as the final code, performing the transfer at an intermediate code distance to shrink early-stage spatial overhead, and a lookup table of error syndromes enabling early rejection of bad shots. Numerics at color-code distance 3 and physical error rate 1e-3 match the original protocol's logical error rate (~3e-6) at about half the space-time cost.
why_it_matters: It makes cultivation compatible with standard lattice-surgery toolchains and the rotated surface code, simplifying integration into full fault-tolerant architectures. It is the lattice-surgery-native cultivation variant, directly connecting the cultivation story to the lattice surgery canon.

title: Constant depth magic state cultivation with Clifford measurements by gauging
authors: Bence Hetényi, Benjamin J. Brown, Dominic J. Williamson
one_sentence: Uses gauging of a transversal Clifford gate to measure the color code's logical Clifford operator in constant circuit depth, making cultivation practical beyond distance 5.
contribution: Replaces the O(d)-depth logical Clifford measurement of standard magic state cultivation with a constant-depth measurement obtained by gauging the color code's transversal Clifford gate, which temporarily produces an emergent Clifford stabilizer code. Rather than error-correcting that emergent code, the protocol repeats gauging measurements with post-selection, trading scalability for simplicity, and works on a regular square-grid connectivity. The d=7 version reaches the 1e-12 logical-error-rate regime at 0.05% physical error rate while keeping more than 1% of shots after the cultivation-equivalent stage—territory inaccessible to the original d<=5-limited protocol.
why_it_matters: It removes the depth bottleneck that capped cultivation at distance 5, opening the route to the ultra-low logical error rates needed for large-scale algorithms. It demonstrates how the gauging-based logical-measurement toolkit feeds directly into cheaper magic state preparation.

title: Zero-level CCZ Distillation
authors: Tomohiro Itogawa, Yutaka Hirano, Yutaro Akahoshi, Keisuke Fujii
one_sentence: Distills a high-fidelity CCZ magic state directly from physical qubits using the transversal T of the [[8,3,2]] code and lattice surgery, with no logical-level distillation overhead.
contribution: Extends the zero-level distillation paradigm from T states to CCZ states: the transversal T/T-dagger of the [[8,3,2]] code fault-tolerantly encodes CCZ|+++, which is then teleported onto three surface-code logical qubits via lattice surgery. A new 'adaptively initialized teleportation' (AIT) procedure handles teleportation between codes of different distances. The full circuit needs only 22 physical qubits, 3 logical qubits, and depth 24, achieving p_L ~ 300 p^2—one to two orders of magnitude better than seven-T-gate constructions at p = 1e-3 to 1e-4 and a 5-10x space-time reduction over prior methods.
why_it_matters: It shows the cultivation/zero-level philosophy extends beyond T states to the CCZ states that power Toffoli-heavy algorithms, sharpening the physical-level alternative to logical-level distillation factories. Together with its companion cultivation work, it maps out a cheap magic-state menu for early fault-tolerant machines.

title: A Game of Surface Codes: Large-Scale Quantum Computing with Lattice Surgery
authors: Daniel Litinski
one_sentence: A tile-based rulebook for compiling arbitrary quantum circuits onto surface-code patches with lattice surgery, quantifying space-time trade-offs from small to huge machines.
contribution: Systematizes large-patch lattice surgery compilation: surface-code patches are treated as tiles with a small set of merge/split and measurement rules, and circuits are executed as sequences of multi-qubit Pauli measurements consuming distilled magic states. It gives explicit space-time volume estimates across regimes—e.g., a classically intractable 100-qubit, 1e8-T-count computation in 4 hours on 55,000 qubits or 22 minutes on 120,000 qubits at 1e-4 physical error rate. The framework popularized fast data blocks, compact blocks, and the space-time-cost accounting that all later resource estimates build on.
why_it_matters: It is the canonical large-patch lattice surgery compilation reference: the cost model in which magic state factories—including cultivation and zero-level distillation—are ultimately judged. Every cultivation variant's space-time-overhead claims are measured against the factory footprint this paper defines. Published as Quantum 3, 128 (2019).
